newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania president cuts deal, must persuade rebels.
newsitem.headline: Albania president cuts deal, must persuade rebels.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha reached a deal with his political opponents to resolve the Balkan country's crisis but must now persuade insurgents in the south to lay down their weapons and abide by its provisions.

The nine-point accord, signed after two days of talks and mediation by senior European emissaries, calls for the formation of an interim government from all major parties to oversee elections to be held by June.
Negotiations were to begin immediately on distributing portfolios. Opposition politicians predicted a battle posts with Berisha's right-wing Democratic Party over the key security posts.
The insurgents controlling many towns in the volatile south after more than a month of civil disturbances were sceptical. Some pledged to hold out for Berisha's resignation.

Ex-general Agim Gozhita, the rebel leader in Gjirokaster, a garrison town 30 km (20 miles) from the Greek border, said he was pleased with the agreement and was conferring with other rebel-held towns.
The deal extended for a week an amnesty for rebel fighters if they gave up their arms, but Gozhita said: "At this point our position remains that Berisha must quit before we surrender our weapons."

Berisha had previously vehemently opposed any coalition with the Socialists, heirs to the communists who ran a repressive regime for 45 years but have since formally renounced Marxism. He said his party's statutes forbade deals with ex-communists.

"Last night I was categorical about the Socialist Party," he said after the deal, referring to tough talks overseen by two European missions. "But there are moral considerations...a moral obligation. Sometimes, you have to choose morals over laws."

Paskal Milo, of the opposition Social Democrats, described the pact as "a very important first step. There may be some problems when we start dividing up ministries. You can imagine that jobs like the Interior Ministry are important."

Politicians who had accused Berisha of steering the country towards authoritarian rule after his Democrats won nearly all the seats in last May's contested election praised his moral stand in accepting the deal.

The June deadline for elections was a boon for the opposition. Berisha had proposed holding elections within 45 days, but the opposition said no poll could be staged so quickly under emergency rule introduced last week.
One Socialist in Tirana, Pandeli Majko, said he was ready to go with a Democratic Party leader to the south to win over the rebels.
But a Socialist in the rebel "defence council" of Gjirokaster said his party would demand the release of its leader Fatos Nano, jailed in 1994 on corruption charges.
Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini, who briefly visited Tirana, said the rebels "have no legitimacy. This is a good beginning for establishing peace. Everyone wants Italy to be a guarantor."
Mass protests in the south grw into open anti-government revolt after first erupting in January over losses suffered by hundreds of thousands of people when dubious investment schemes collapsed.

More than 20 people have died in the violence in the past week. Parliament first imposed a state of emergency and then re-elected Berisha to a second five-year term, enraging the opposition and dismaying foreign countries.

One of the first casualties of the changing political climate was Quemal Sakajeva, director of Albania's staid state television. An announcement said he resigned on Sunday "after five years of tiring work."
